nodes.title: The flag scheme
nodes.statement: Let F be the scheme representing the fppf quotient G/B. The quotient map G→F is a right B-torsor, and its functor of points is the sheafification of S↦G(S)/B(S), rather than the naive quotient on every S. Fix the base flag eB and the left G-action.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: Use the representable parabolic quotient supplied by ReductiveGroups; identify its universal B-torsor and descend the left action.
Keep the fppf sheaf quotient in the universal property: points over a test scheme need only lift to G locally.
acceptance: For G=T and B=T, F=Spec k.
For SL₂ with upper triangular B, F≅P¹ and eB corresponds to the line ke₁.
For GL₃, points are a line inside a plane in k³; choosing only a line loses one flag parameter.

nodes.title: Smooth projectivity of the flag variety
nodes.statement: F is smooth, projective and geometrically integral over k, of dimension N=dim U; D=dim G=r+2N and dim B=r+N, where r=dim T. These dimension equalities persist after extension of k.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: Use the big Bruhat cell, a product of the negative root subgroups, to obtain a smooth dense affine N-space; translate it to cover F.
The parabolic quotient is proper and admits a projective embedding using a regular dominant character that belongs to X*(T); do not assume ρ itself is an integral character.
The dense cell over an algebraic closure proves geometric integrality; the root decomposition gives the dimensions.
acceptance: F is smooth, projective and geometrically integral over k, of dimension N=dim U; D=dim G=r+2N and dim B=r+N, where r=dim T. These dimension equalities persist after extension of k.
For SL₂, F=P¹ has dimension 1, B has dimension 2 and G has dimension 3; for a torus F is a point and D=r.

nodes.statement: For w∈W=N_G(T)/T, choose a representative ŵ and let U_w⊂F×F be the diagonal G-orbit of (eB,ŵB), with its locally closed reduced orbit scheme. Define Ū_w as its reduced closed closure. These constructions are independent of ŵ.

proofSteps: Identify the orbit with G/(B∩ŵBŵ⁻¹) and descend its orbit map.
Take the reduced closure in F×F and use the Bruhat decomposition to identify its support.

For SL₂, U_s consists of pairs of distinct lines, and Ū_s=P¹×P¹.
For a torus W={e}, the sole orbit and its closure are Spec k.

nodes.title: Intersection of subvector bundles
nodes.statement: Let Y be reduced and locally of finite type over a field, E a finite-rank vector bundle, and E₁,E₂ subvector bundles (locally direct summands). If dim(E₁,y∩E₂,y)=a for every closed y∈Y, their scheme theoretic intersection in E is a vector subbundle of rank a, with fibre the intersection of the two fibres. No assertion is made over a nonreduced base.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: Locally identify the intersection with ker(E₁⊕E₂→E), (x,y)↦x−y.
Constant fibre ranks at closed points give constant ranks everywhere because finite-type schemes over a field are Jacobson. Minors that vanish at every closed point vanish on the reduced base.
On the open where a maximal nonzero minor is invertible, row and column operations split the map into an identity block and zero block; the kernel is locally free and a direct summand.
acceptance: Let Y be reduced and locally of finite type over a field, E a finite-rank vector bundle, and E₁,E₂ subvector bundles (locally direct summands). If dim(E₁,y∩E₂,y)=a for every closed y∈Y, their scheme theoretic intersection in E is a vector subbundle of rank a, with fibre the intersection of the two fibres. No assertion is made over a nonreduced base.

Over k[ε]/ε², the summands spanned by (1,0) and (1,ε) in the free rank-two module have one-dimensional intersection on the closed fibre, but their actual intersection is (ε)(1,0), not a rank-one direct summand. The reduced-base hypothesis must reject this case.

sources.match: Reducedness and constant closed-fibre rank make the intersection a geometric vector bundle.

nodes.title: The Grothendieck simultaneous resolution
nodes.statement: Define g̃=G×ᴮb using (g,x)∼(gb,Ad(b⁻¹)x). Identify it with the closed incidence scheme {(gB,ψ)∈F×g:Ad(g⁻¹)ψ∈b}. The bundle projection is p:g̃→F, and q:g̃→g sends (gB,ψ) to ψ.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: Descend the B-representation b along G→F using the existing vector-bundle theory.
The inclusion b→g descends to a subbundle of F×g, and (g,x)↦(gB,Ad(g)x) gives the incidence comparison.
Define q by the ambient projection and prove the formula independently of the torsor representative.
acceptance: For a torus F is a point, g̃=t and q=id.
For GL₂, an incidence point is a line L⊂k² and a matrix preserving L; p has rank 3.
q⁻¹(0)=F scheme theoretically, whereas g̃ itself has dimension D.

nodes.title: Regular and regular semisimple loci
nodes.statement: Use the reductive Lie-algebra Jordan decomposition. An element ψ is regular when its algebraic centralizer has dimension r. It is regular semisimple when it is both regular and semisimple. Write gʳᵉᵍ and gʳˢ for these open subschemes, and g̃ʳᵉᵍ,q⁻¹(gʳˢ) for their scheme inverse images. Set tʳᵉᵍ=t∩gʳˢ.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: Express regularity by the minimal centralizer dimension and construct the corresponding open locus.
Identify the semisimple regular locus by conjugating t minus the root hyperplanes; the Jordan-theory input and its characteristic bound are explicit.
acceptance: For a torus every Lie-algebra element is regular semisimple.
For SL₂ in characteristic different from 2, the nonzero nilpotent matrix E₁₂ is regular and is not semisimple.
For SL₂, zero is not regular, whereas diag(a,−a) is regular semisimple when a≠0.

nodes.title: Properness and the regular covering
nodes.statement: The scheme g̃ is smooth and geometrically integral of dimension D. The map q is proper and surjective; q⁻¹(gʳᵉᵍ)→gʳᵉᵍ is quasi-finite (hence finite), and q⁻¹(gʳˢ)→gʳˢ is finite étale of constant degree |W|.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: Smoothness and dimension follow from the bundle of rank dim B over F. Closed incidence in F×g gives properness.
Every geometric Lie-algebra element is contained in a Borel subalgebra; this proves surjectivity.

The regular-element Borel-finiteness theorem gives quasi-finiteness. Over a regular semisimple element the Borels containing its centralizer torus form the W-torsor; root-coordinate differentials prove étaleness. The Lie-theoretic proof boundary is recorded.
acceptance: The scheme g̃ is smooth and geometrically integral of dimension D. The map q is proper and surjective; q⁻¹(gʳᵉᵍ)→gʳᵉᵍ is quasi-finite (hence finite), and q⁻¹(gʳˢ)→gʳˢ is finite étale of constant degree |W|.

For SL₂, the regular semisimple fibre has two flags, while a regular nonzero nilpotent has one geometric flag. The latter statement is not a claim of étaleness there; q is ramified and is not birational.

nodes.title: Local complete intersection of X
nodes.statement: The X_w, w∈W, are exactly the irreducible components of X; X is equidimensional of dimension D and is a local complete intersection over k, hence Cohen–Macaulay. This statement concerns X and does not yet prove CM for the separate reduced X_w.

proofSteps: The finite stratum decomposition shows the closures exhaust the components.
X lies in the smooth scheme F×F×g of dimension D+2N. Each incidence condition is the vanishing of a section of the rank-N quotient of the Borel subbundle.
Locally X is cut out by 2N equations with codimension 2N; the expected-codimension criterion in a regular local ring makes them a regular sequence. Import the general CI-to-CM theorem.

nodes.title: Reducedness of X
nodes.statement: X is reduced. Its generic points lie above gʳˢ, and each reduced component X_w therefore agrees with its component scheme structure obtained from the generically reduced CM scheme X.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.

For each V_w its restriction to regular semisimple ψ is nonempty and dense: take a regular toral element in its fibre.
The fibre product of the finite étale regular semisimple covering is étale over its smooth base and hence reduced; it contains all generic points of X.

nodes.title: Birational projections of the components
nodes.statement: For i=1,2, pr_i,w:X_w→g̃ is proper birational and restricts to an isomorphism above g̃ʳᵉᵍ. In particular that inverse-image open of X_w is smooth. The full q is not asserted birational when W is nontrivial.

nodes.title: Dimensions of Cartan fibres
nodes.statement: For each i∈{1,2}, κ_i:X→t and κ_i,w:X_w→t are surjective, and every geometric fibre of each is equidimensional of dimension D−r=2N.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: The dense stratum description gives surjectivity for X_w: its toral coordinate can be prescribed.

At zero, the stratum over U_v has nilpotent-intersection fibre dimension N−ℓ(v), so every stratum in the zero fibre has dimension 2N. The dimension inequality for fibres supplies the matching lower bound for components of X_w.

Use upper semicontinuity on X of the local fibre dimension x↦dim_x κ_i⁻¹(κ_i(x)). Its locus above 2N is closed and scaling-stable. Each scalar orbit extends to zero operator on the same flags, so a nonempty excess-dimension locus would meet the zero fibre, contradicting its stratum calculation. The lower bound on every component then proves equidimensionality. Apply the same argument to each scaling-stable X_w.
acceptance: For each i∈{1,2}, κ_i:X→t and κ_i,w:X_w→t are surjective, and every geometric fibre of each is equidimensional of dimension D−r=2N.
For a torus κ_i=id_t and fibres have dimension 0. For SL₂ both incidence components have every Cartan fibre of dimension 2, including the zero fibre with its possibly multiple components.

nodes.title: Bezrukavnikov–Riche Cohen–Macaulay theorem
nodes.statement: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p>h, for a semisimple simply connected split G, the reduced graph closures X_w are Cohen–Macaulay. In the integral model over Z_(p), formation of these closures commutes with the special fibre: X_A,w×F_p=X_Fp,w scheme theoretically. The BR coadjoint and inverse-index conventions are translated before applying this input.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: BR works with annihilators in g* and labels the orbit by w⁻¹. Use an invariant form in this characteristic range and replace w by w⁻¹ to compare the closures.

Read BR Theorem 2.2.1 as the stated CM input. Its proof identifies the structure sheaf with a derived convolution kernel by Bruhat induction; the required positive-characteristic localisation and kernel-concentration package is the explicit BR-input gap, not a theorem claimed to be available in Lean.
Use BR Remark 2.11.1 for the actual scheme special fibre; topological equality would not suffice.

In the integral model over Z_(p), formation of these closures commutes with the special fibre: X_A,w×F_p=X_Fp,w scheme theoretically. The BR coadjoint and inverse-index conventions are translated before applying this input.
For type A₁ in characteristic 5, h=2 and the input applies to both labels. Verify the scheme special fibre of the closure, rather than just equality of its underlying set.

CM graph closures arise from convolution kernels, with scheme theoretic base change over large primes.

nodes.title: Cohen–Macaulayness in the required generality
nodes.statement: For split connected reductive G and char(k)=0 or p>h, every X_w is geometrically Cohen–Macaulay. In characteristic zero, choose p>h and the split Chevalley model over A=Z_(p); the closure X_A,w is A-flat and has special fibre X_Fp,w.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: After passing to an algebraic closure, replace G by G_der^sc×Z(G)° through a central isogeny of degree invertible in the stated range. Its differential and flag map identify the incidence components with the simply connected components times the central Lie-algebra factor. CM is preserved by this smooth affine factor.

In characteristic zero define X_A,w as the closure of its generic stratum inside the Chevalley incidence model. Its coordinate rings are A-torsion-free, hence A-flat; use BR special-fibre compatibility.

At special-fibre points, flatness over the DVR and the CM special fibre imply CM of the total space. For the remaining generic points use the open CM locus and the G_m-action: a hypothetical bad closed generic point is defined over a number field. Choose a DVR over p, extend both flags by projectivity, and multiply ψ by a sufficiently high power of its uniformizer to make the operator integral. The closed G_m-stable model then extends the scaled bad point into its special fibre. The closed non-CM locus would specialize to a non-CM special point, a contradiction. The CM-locus, DVR extension and faithfully flat descent inputs are precisely the CM-spreading gap.
acceptance: For split connected reductive G and char(k)=0 or p>h, every X_w is geometrically Cohen–Macaulay. In characteristic zero, choose p>h and the split Chevalley model over A=Z_(p); the closure X_A,w is A-flat and has special fibre X_Fp,w.

The type A₁ test applies in characteristic 3 as well as characteristic zero, and the torus test is affine space t. The scaling argument must reach generic points outside an arbitrary initial neighbourhood of the special fibre.

nodes.statement: Each κ_i and κ_i,w is flat. nodes.title: Regular points over a single root wall
nodes.statement: Over an algebraic closure, let s_α be a Weyl reflection and v∈W with ℓ(s_αv)>ℓ(v). In the incidence stratum V_v there are regular elements with κ₁ in ker(s_α−id), and they form a nonempty open subset of its inverse image. More precisely choose z on the α-wall and on no distinct root wall, and 0≠c∈k; z+c e_β is regular for the sign β of α lying in the positive roots with v⁻¹β positive.

The centralizer of a generic point of the wall has semisimple rank one; adding a nonzero vector in its root space changes its rank-one part to regular nilpotent. The remaining root spaces have nonzero z-eigenvalue.
The root decomposition computes centralizer dimension r. Openness of regularity and irreducibility from the preceding theorem give a dense regular open.

nodes.title: Normality of the incidence components
nodes.statement: Every X_w is geometrically normal. This theorem does not assert normality of the reducible X or of the nilpotent components Z_w.
hypotheses: G is split connected reductive over k, with B⊃T and U=radᵤ(B); g,b,t,u are their Lie algebras.
Unless characteristic zero is specified, char(k)=0 or char(k)=p>h, where h is the maximum Coxeter number of the simple factors; for a torus take h=0.
proofSteps: CM gives S₂. A codimension-one component C of the boundary has dense intersection with some V_v, v<w. The Cartan relation for w and v puts it above ker(wv⁻¹−id).

Compare the affine-fibre dimension from SM with dim C=D−1. The fixed-space codimension must be one, so wv⁻¹ is a reflection s_α. The irreducible inverse image from SM is precisely the possible boundary component.

The regular-root-wall theorem shows that this C meets the open on which pr_i,w is an isomorphism to smooth g̃ʳᵉᵍ. Thus every height-one generic point is regular. Apply Serre R₁+S₂, and repeat after algebraic closure.

For SL₂ both X_e and X_s are normal even though their union X is reducible and is not normal at their meeting. No normality conclusion about Z_w follows by taking the Cartan zero fibre.

sources.match: The codimension-one boundary is regular and CM supplies the remaining Serre condition.

nodes.title: Chevalley restriction and the nilpotent fibre
nodes.statement: In characteristic zero the adjoint quotient is c=Spec k[g]^G≅Spec k[t]^W=t/W≅Aʳ. Its zero fibre has reduced support equal to the nilpotent elements of g, and is the reduced nilpotent cone 𝒩. The composite g̃→g→c equals g̃→κ t→t/W. A nondegenerate invariant symmetric form g≅g* exists for reductive G; the Killing form alone is not adequate on the centre.
hypotheses: char(k)=0; G is split connected reductive with the fixed B⊃T.
proofSteps: Use restriction of invariant polynomials and the Weyl invariant-polynomial theorem to construct the quotient comparison. Separate the central summand from the semisimple derived summand.
On the Borel, invariant functions depend only on the toral quotient. The zero toral value forces the central component to vanish and the derived component to be nilpotent.

Use the invariant form on the derived summand and any nondegenerate form on the centre. The Lie-invariants gap includes the precise reduced nilpotent-fibre statement, rather than deriving reducedness from its set of points.
acceptance: In characteristic zero the adjoint quotient is c=Spec k[g]^G≅Spec k[t]^W=t/W≅Aʳ. Its zero fibre has reduced support equal to the nilpotent elements of g, and is the reduced nilpotent cone 𝒩. The composite g̃→g→c equals g̃→κ t→t/W. A nondegenerate invariant symmetric form g≅g* exists for reductive G; the Killing form alone is not adequate on the centre.

For GL₂ the quotient coordinates can be trace and determinant, and their zero fibre is the nilpotent cone. The centre gives a direct counterexample to using the Killing form as a nondegenerate reductive form.

sources.match: The characteristic-zero adjoint quotient identifies the nilpotent geometry and Cartan factorisation.

nodes.title: The Springer resolution

hypotheses: char(k)=0; G is split connected reductive.
proofSteps: Descend u⊂b and compare its associated bundle with the scheme zero fibre of b→t.

The incidence projection is proper, and nilpotent elements admit compatible Borel flags. The regular nilpotent locus has a unique such flag, yielding birationality. The nilpotent-orbit input is kept in Lie-invariants.

For SL₂, 𝒩̃≅Tot O_(P¹)(−2), of dimension 2.

A covector annihilates the diagonal orbit tangent exactly when the two moment maps add to zero. Use a minus sign in the first factor and the identity in the second.

nodes.title: Kashiwara equivalence
nodes.statement: For a closed immersion i:W→Y of smooth varieties, i_+ is exact on quasi-coherent D-modules and induces an equivalence from D_W-modules to D_Y-modules supported set theoretically on W, with inverse H⁰(i†), where i†=Li*[−codim_Y W]. This equivalence restricts to coherent modules. In normal coordinates, the direct image consists of finite sums of normal derivative monomials applied to the original module.
hypotheses: k is a field of characteristic zero; Y is a smooth separated finite-type k-scheme of pure dimension n.
All D-modules are left modules with quasi-coherent underlying O_Y-module; coherent means finite over D_Y, not necessarily finite over O_Y.
proofSteps: Locally reduce to coordinate subspaces. The relations between the normal coordinates and normal derivatives give the expansion and identify sections killed by the normal ideal.

Use induction on the normal multi-index to prove full faithfulness and essential surjectivity. Patch these coordinate equivalences. The full sheaf/homological proof is bounded by the D-homological input gap.
acceptance: For a closed immersion i:W→Y of smooth varieties, i_+ is exact on quasi-coherent D-modules and induces an equivalence from D_W-modules to D_Y-modules supported set theoretically on W, with inverse H⁰(i†), where i†=Li*[−codim_Y W]. This equivalence restricts to coherent modules. In normal coordinates, the direct image consists of finite sums of normal derivative monomials applied to the original module.
For {0}→A¹, the direct image of k is k[∂] with x acting by lowering derivatives; ker x=k and coker x=0. Thus Li*[−1] recovers k in degree zero.

nodes.title: Finite holonomic length and cycle additivity
nodes.statement: Every holonomic D_Y-module has finite length. For every short exact sequence 0→M′→M→M″→0 of holonomic modules, CC(M)=CC(M′)+CC(M″). Hence CC defines a group homomorphism from K₀(Hol(D_Y)) to the free group on n-dimensional characteristic components.
hypotheses: k is a field of characteristic zero; Y is a smooth separated finite-type k-scheme of pure dimension n.
All D-modules are left modules with quasi-coherent underlying O_Y-module; coherent means finite over D_Y, not necessarily finite over O_Y.
proofSteps: Use induced good filtrations to obtain an exact sequence of coherent graded modules. At each top generic point apply native module-length additivity.

The characteristic support of any subquotient lies in the finite union of components of Ch(M), and a nonzero holonomic subquotient contributes a positive coefficient somewhere. Total multiplicity therefore bounds every strict ascending or descending chain, proving finite length.
The exact-sequence relation is precisely the defining relation of K₀, so additivity supplies the homomorphism.
acceptance: Every holonomic D_Y-module has finite length. For every short exact sequence 0→M′→M→M″→0 of holonomic modules, CC(M)=CC(M′)+CC(M″). Hence CC defines a group homomorphism from K₀(Hol(D_Y)) to the free group on n-dimensional characteristic components.
For δ₀⊕δ₀ on A¹ the finite length is 2 and its cycle is twice the cotangent fibre. Additivity must retain this coefficient for extensions too, rather than counting only reduced support components.

nodes.title: Regular holonomic D-modules
nodes.statement: An integrable connection is regular if every restriction to a smooth locally closed curve has, at every boundary point of a smooth projective completion, a logarithmic lattice. A simple holonomic module is regular if it is j_!* of a simple regular connection on a smooth locally closed support. A holonomic module is regular when all its simple factors are regular. Use the simple-module classification to transfer the curve condition to simple holonomic objects. Extend through finite composition series; Jordan–Hölder makes this independent of the series.

nodes.title: Moment-map support and orbit classification
nodes.statement: For a strongly H-equivariant coherent D_Y-module M, Ch(M) lies in the zero fibre of the cotangent moment map μ_H:T*Y→Lie(H)*. Over an algebraically closed k, when H acts with finitely many orbits and geometrically connected stabilizers on Y, the strongly H-equivariant regular holonomic simple objects are exactly the intermediate extensions of trivial rank-one connections on individual orbits. For the diagonal G-action on F×F their reduced characteristic support lies in the signed Steinberg variety.
hypotheses: k is a field of characteristic zero; Y is a smooth separated finite-type k-scheme of pure dimension n.
All D-modules are left modules with quasi-coherent underlying O_Y-module; coherent means finite over D_Y, not necessarily finite over O_Y.

H is smooth. The finite-orbit simple classification is asserted over an algebraically closed field with geometrically connected stabilizers; the moment-support inclusion needs neither restriction. General-field comparisons are the D-regular input.
proofSteps: Choose an equivariant good filtration locally. Differentiated compatibility makes infinitesimal orbit vector fields act on gr M with zero principal symbol; hence their moment functions annihilate the support.

On a transitive orbit, strong equivariance identifies equivariant connections with representations of the stabilizer component group. Connected stabilizers give only trivial simples. Use intermediate extension and finite-length induction.
Apply the moment-map assertion to the diagonal G-action on F×F and use the signed conormal description of Z. The separate induction equivalence is constructed in L/equivariant-induction.
acceptance: For a strongly H-equivariant coherent D_Y-module M, Ch(M) lies in the zero fibre of the cotangent moment map μ_H:T*Y→Lie(H)*. Over an algebraically closed k, when H acts with finitely many orbits and geometrically connected stabilizers on Y, the strongly H-equivariant regular holonomic simple objects are exactly the intermediate extensions of trivial rank-one connections on individual orbits. For the diagonal G-action on F×F their reduced characteristic support lies in the signed Steinberg variety.

For the diagonal action on P¹×P¹ there are exactly two orbits with connected stabilizers. Their trivial rank-one connections yield the two equivariant simples, whose characteristic supports are in the signed Steinberg variety.

nodes.title: Beilinson–Bernstein localisation
nodes.statement: Define Loc(M)=D_F⊗_(U_χ₀)M, with the tensor sheafified, for a U_χ₀-module M. The functors Loc and Γ(F,−) are mutually inverse exact equivalences between U_χ₀-modules and O-quasi-coherent D_F-modules. They restrict to finitely generated modules and coherent D_F-modules. hypotheses: The hypotheses and central-character conventions of L/flag-d-affinity hold.
proofSteps: Use the global U_χ₀-action on D_F to construct the tensor functor. The natural unit and evaluation counit form an adjunction. For split reductive g, use the derived semisimple algebra and the prescribed scalar action of the centre; this extension of the semisimple upstream Verma/central-character interfaces is retained in CategoryO-elementary.

D-affinity makes Γ exact and conservative, while global generation makes the counit surjective. Apply the same argument to its kernel and to presentations by free modules to prove both unit and counit are isomorphisms.

nodes.title: The components of the Cartan fibre product
nodes.statement: The irreducible components of 𝒯 are the distinct smooth graphs 𝒯_w≅t. In characteristic zero 𝒯 is reduced and equidimensional of dimension r. The graphs may meet; no disjoint-union assertion is made.
hypotheses: char(k)=0; Chevalley invariant-polynomial theorem is available.
proofSteps: The finite quotient t→t/W separates W-orbits of geometric points, so the support is the union of the graphs. Generic points away from the reflecting hyperplanes distinguish them.
Polynomial invariants give 𝒯 as r equations in smooth t×t with expected codimension r. It is therefore CM, and it is generically étale over t. CM plus generic reducedness gives reducedness.

nodes.title: Detection of components after completion
nodes.statement: Let x be a closed point of X_w, and y=κ(x)∈𝒯_w. The map of completed local schemes (X_w)^∧_x→𝒯^∧_y factors through (𝒯_(w′))^∧_y if and only if w′=w. When y∉𝒯_(w′), that closed subscheme has empty completion and cannot contain the nonempty source. The generic point used in the proof lies on 𝒯_w, not on X.
hypotheses: char(k)=0; x is closed and belongs to X_w.
proofSteps: Normality and excellence make the completion of the local ring of X_w normal and integral. Its map to the smooth graph is induced by the flat surjective Cartan map, and remains schematically dominant after completion.

If it factored through a distinct graph, that dominance would put all of 𝒯_w in its intersection with 𝒯_(w′), contradicting distinct graph generic points. Faithful flatness of local completion preserves the nonempty dense image.
Record separately the standard excellent-normal-completion and completion-flatness comparisons; their native scheme application lies in AG-geometry.
